title: H-1B to Canadian PR Transition: RSU Tax Planning Guide to Save $20K+ in 2026
description: Strategic tax planning for H-1B workers transitioning to Canadian PR with unvested RSUs. Learn timing optimization, treaty benefits, and avoid the $35K double taxation trap.
content:
## Key Takeaways

- **Timing matters:** Leaving 1 month earlier/later can save **$15,000-$30,000** in taxes
- Canadian PR approval doesn't = tax residency (you control the trigger date)
- **Accelerated vesting** before leaving US eliminates 4 years of dual-country filing
- Average savings with proper planning: **$23,000** per $100K unvested RSUs
- Use our [free calculator](/us-canada-tax-calculator) to model optimal departure timing

## Understanding the H-1B to PR Tax Transition

### The Two Key Dates That Determine Your Taxes

**Date 1: Canadian PR Approval**
- IRCC (Immigration Canada) approves your PR application
- You receive Confirmation of Permanent Residence (COPR)
- **Important:** PR approval ≠ tax residency

**Date 2: Tax Residency Establishment**
- You physically land in Canada AND establish "residential ties"
- Residential ties: buy/rent home, move spouse/dependents, open bank accounts
- **This is the trigger for worldwide taxation**

**Example:**
- PR approved: Jan 1, 2026
- You stay in US working: Jan-June 2026
- You land in Canada: July 1, 2026
- **Tax residency begins: July 1, 2026** (not Jan 1)

**Why this matters:**
- RSUs vesting Jan-June: **100% US tax only** (you're US resident)
- RSUs vesting July-Dec: **US + Canada tax** (dual taxation risk)

### The $35,000 Double Taxation Trap

**Scenario:** You transition without planning

**Profile:**
- H-1B at Meta Menlo Park: 2022-2025 (3 years)
- PR approved: Dec 2025
- Landed in Toronto: Jan 2026 (excited to start new life)
- Unvested RSUs: $320,000 over 4 years ($80K/year)

**What happens:**

**2026-2029 (Years 2-5 of RSU grant):**
- Each year: $80,000 vests
- US portion (based on work period): 75% = $60,000
- Canada portion: 25% = $20,000

**Annual tax:**
- US tax: $60K × 22% = $13,200
- Canada tax: $80K × 35% = $28,000
- Canada FTC: -$13,200
- **Net tax: $27,800/year**

**Over 4 years:** $111,200 total tax

**If you had stayed in US (no PR):**
- US tax only: $80K × 28% = $22,400/year
- Over 4 years: **$89,600**
- **Difference: $21,600 extra** (24% more tax)

**Plus administrative burden:**
- Dual-country filing for 4 years
- CPA fees: $2,500/year × 4 = **$10,000**
- Total extra cost: $21,600 + $10,000 = **$31,600**

## Optimal Timing Strategies

### Strategy 1: Delay PR Landing Until After Major Vesting

If you have a large RSU vesting scheduled, delay your Canadian tax residency.

**Example:**

**Facts:**
- PR approved: Sept 2025
- COPR expires: Sept 2026 (1 year to land)
- Large RSU vesting: March 2026 ($150,000)
- Normal annual vesting: $50,000 (Sept each year)

**Option A: Land immediately (Sept 2025)**
- March 2026 vesting: Dual taxation (US + Canada)
- US tax: $150K × 100% (all earned in US) × 22% = $33,000
- Canada tax: $150K × 35% = $52,500
- Canada FTC: -$33,000
- **Net: $52,500**

**Option B: Land after vesting (April 2026)**
- March 2026 vesting: US tax only (not yet Canadian resident)
- US tax: $150K × 28% = **$42,000**
- Canada tax: $0
- **Net: $42,000**
- **Savings: $10,500** (20% less)

**Plus:**
- Simpler filing (no dual-country for 2026)
- No FTC complexity
- **Total value: $10,500 + $2,500 CPA fee = $13,000**

**Risk:**
- COPR expires Sept 2026 (must land before then)
- H-1B might not extend past March 2026

### Strategy 2: Accelerate Vesting Before Leaving

Some employers (Meta, Amazon, Stripe) allow early vesting when you leave.

**How it works:**
- You give notice: leaving for Canada
- Unvested RSUs: $240,000 over 3 years
- HR offers: "Vest everything now" (last day of work)
- You accept: All $240,000 vests in final paycheck

**Tax impact:**

**Without acceleration:**
- Year 1: $80K vests → US + Canada tax = $27,800
- Year 2: $80K vests → US + Canada tax = $27,800
- Year 3: $80K vests → US + Canada tax = $27,800
- **Total: $83,400** (over 3 years)

**With acceleration:**
- Final paycheck: $240K vests → US tax only = $88,800 (37% marginal)
- Years 1-3: $0 vests → No filing needed
- **Total: $88,800** (one-time)

**Analysis:**
- Acceleration costs $5,400 more in immediate tax (37% vs 28% effective)
- But saves:
  - $7,500 in CPA fees (3 years × $2,500)
  - $2,000 in FX risk (CAD might strengthen)
  - Opportunity cost (invest $240K immediately vs waiting 3 years)
- **Net benefit: ~$4,100**

**Plus intangibles:**
- Clean break (no ties to US employer)
- No dual-country filing headaches
- Cash in hand (can invest in Canadian real estate immediately)

**Downside:**
- Large tax bill in final year (need $88,800 cash)
- Stock might appreciate (miss 3 years of gains)

### Strategy 3: Establish "Soft Landing" (Maintain US Residency)

You can land in Canada to activate PR but **not become a tax resident** yet.

**How it works:**
1. Land in Canada (activate PR before COPR expires)
2. Spend <183 days/year in Canada
3. Maintain **primary residential ties in US** (keep H-1B, apartment, etc.)
4. Delay establishing Canadian ties (don't buy home, don't bring spouse)

**Tax result:**
- You're a **non-resident** of Canada for tax purposes
- Canada doesn't tax your worldwide income
- US taxes only (as H-1B resident)

**Example:**

**2026:**
- Land in Canada: Feb 1 (activate PR)
- Stay in US working: Feb-Dec (334 days)
- Visit Canada: 31 days total
- **Tax residency: US** (under 183-day test)

**2027:**
- Work in US: Jan-Aug (244 days)
- All RSUs vest: $320,000 (Jan vesting)
- US tax: $320K × 35% = $112,000
- Canada tax: $0 (non-resident)
- Move to Canada permanently: Sept 2027

**Savings:**
- Avoided dual taxation on $320K
- Saved ~$20,000 in extra Canada tax
- Delayed PR obligations by 18 months (gave yourself optionality)

**Risks:**
- CRA might challenge non-residency (if you have spouse/kids in Canada)
- Must file Form NR73 (Determination of Residency Status) to prove non-residency
- If deemed resident: Owe back taxes + penalties

**Best for:**
- Single filers (no spouse to tie you to Canada)
- Large unvested RSUs (>$500K)
- Flexible work arrangements (can stay in US 1-2 more years)

### Strategy 4: Negotiate Remote Work from Canada

Some US employers allow Canadian remote work for H-1B → PR transitions.

**How it works:**
1. You become Canadian PR
2. Employer agrees to keep you as employee (remote from Canada)
3. You work from Canada but still on US payroll
4. Employer withholds **both** US and Canadian tax

**Tax treatment:**
- Canada taxes your employment income (you're resident)
- US taxes your employment income (effectively connected)
- You claim Foreign Tax Credit in Canada for US tax paid
- **Net: Similar to dual-country RSU taxation** (but clean)

**Example:**

**2026 income:**
- Salary: $180,000 (working from Toronto for Meta)
- RSU vesting: $80,000
- Total: $260,000

**US tax:**
- Employer withholds: 25% = $65,000

**Canada tax:**
- Gross tax: $260K × 35% = $91,000
- Less US FTC: $65,000
- **Net: $26,000 CAD**

**Total tax: $65,000 (US) + $26,000 CAD = ~$84,000** (32% effective)

**Benefits:**
- Keep US salary (often 30% higher than Canadian equivalent)
- Keep vesting RSUs (don't forfeit unvested equity)
- Clean tax treatment (employer handles withholding)

**Challenges:**
- Few employers allow this (Meta, Google sometimes do; Amazon rarely)
- Work permit issues (TN no longer valid; must be on Canadian PR)
- Employer must register in Canada (payroll tax complications)

## Cross-Border Tax Residency Rules

### Canada Residency Tests

You become a Canadian tax resident when you have **significant residential ties**:

**Primary ties (one of these makes you resident):**
- ✅ Home in Canada (owned or rented)
- ✅ Spouse/common-law partner in Canada
- ✅ Dependents in Canada

**Secondary ties (multiple = resident):**
- Personal property in Canada (car, furniture)
- Social ties (join clubs, gym membership)
- Economic ties (Canadian bank accounts, credit cards)
- Canadian driver's license
- Health insurance (provincial coverage)

**Example:**

**Scenario A: Clear Canadian resident**
- Bought condo in Toronto: ✅ (primary tie)
- Moved spouse and kids: ✅ (primary tie)
- **Result: Canadian resident from move-in date**

**Scenario B: Non-resident (soft landing)**
- Visit Canada 2 weeks/month (Airbnb hotels)
- Spouse/kids remain in US
- No Canadian home/car/bank account
- **Result: NOT Canadian resident** (even with PR status)

**Form to file:** NR73 (Determination of Residency Status) - CRA confirms your status

### US Residency Tests

You remain a US tax resident until you fail the **Substantial Presence Test**:

**Formula:**
```
Days in US this year
+ 1/3 × days in US last year
+ 1/6 × days in US 2 years ago
≥ 183 days → US resident
```

**Example:**

**2026:**
- Days in US: 180 (Jan-June working)

**2025:**
- Days in US: 365 (full year H-1B)

**2024:**
- Days in US: 365

**Calculation:**
- 180 + (365/3) + (365/6) = 180 + 122 + 61 = **363 days**
- Result: **US resident** for 2026 (even though you left in June)

**How to break US residency:**
- Spend <183 days over 3-year weighted period
- File Form 8840 (Closer Connection to Foreign Country)
- Demonstrate Canadian ties > US ties

**Dual-status year:**
- Part of year: US resident
- Part of year: Canadian resident
- File: US Form 1040 (dual-status statement) + Canada T1

## Real Case Study: Amazon H-1B → PR Transition

**Profile:**
- Sarah, SWE at Amazon Seattle
- H-1B: 2021-2025 (4 years)
- PR approved: July 2025
- Unvested RSUs: $400,000 (4-year grants, $100K/year vesting)

**Option A: Move immediately (Aug 2025)**

**Tax impact (2025-2028):**
- Each year: $100K vests
- US portion: 75% = $75K (worked 3 of 4 years in US)
- Canada portion: 25% = $25K

**Annual tax:**
- US: $75K × 22% = $16,500
- Canada: $100K × 35% = $35,000 CAD
- FTC: -$16,500 = -$22,440 CAD
- Net Canada: $12,560 CAD = $9,235 USD
- **Total: $25,735/year**

**Over 4 years:**
- Total tax: $102,940
- CPA fees: $10,000 (4 years × $2,500)
- **Total cost: $112,940**

**Option B: Delay move until after all vesting (2029)**

**Tax impact:**
- 2025-2028: US resident
- Each year: $100K vests
- US tax only: $100K × 28% = $28,000/year
- Over 4 years: **$112,000**

**Analysis:**
- Option A: $112,940 total
- Option B: $112,000 total
- **Difference: $940** (negligible)

**But:** Option B requires staying in US 4 more years (family/life considerations)

**Option C: Accelerate vesting + move immediately**

Sarah negotiates with Amazon:
- Quit date: Aug 2025
- Amazon vests all remaining RSUs: $300,000 (3 years early)
- Final paycheck: $300,000 vesting

**Tax (2025):**
- $300K at 35% marginal = **$105,000** (one-time)
- 2026-2028: $0 vesting → no filing

**Total cost:**
- Tax: $105,000
- CPA: $0 (no dual-country filing)
- **Total: $105,000**

**Comparison:**
- Option A (move immediately, normal vesting): $112,940
- Option B (delay move): $112,000
- Option C (accelerate + move): **$105,000**
- **Winner: Option C saves $7,940** (7% less total tax)

**Plus intangibles:**
- Sarah gets $300K cash immediately (can invest)
- Moves to Canada right away (family priority)
- No 4 years of dual filing headaches

**Decision:** Sarah chose Option C.

## Tax Treaty Benefits (Article XV)

### How the US-Canada Treaty Allocates RSU Income

**Article XV(1): Employment Income**
> "Salaries, wages and other similar remuneration derived by a resident of a Contracting State in respect of an employment shall be taxable only in that State unless the employment is exercised in the other Contracting State."

**What this means for RSUs:**
- RSUs are "deferred compensation" for employment services
- Taxed based on where you **performed the work** (not where they vest)
- Allocated proportionally using work period formula

**Work period formula:**
```
Country X portion = Total RSU × (Days worked in Country X / Total vesting period)
```

**Example:**
- 4-year grant: Jan 1, 2023 - Jan 1, 2027 (1,461 days)
- Worked in US: Jan 2023 - June 2025 (912 days)
- Worked in Canada: July 2025 - Jan 2027 (549 days)

**Allocation:**
- US portion: $100K × (912 / 1,461) = **$62,423**
- Canada portion: $100K × (549 / 1,461) = **$37,577**

**Tax treatment:**
- US can tax: $62,423 (you worked there)
- Canada can tax: $100,000 (you're resident when it vests)
- Canada gives FTC for US tax on $62,423
- **Net: Canada taxes $37,577 after credit**

### Form 8833: Claiming Treaty Benefits

To claim Article XV benefits, you must file **Form 8833** with your US return.

**When required:**
- Treaty benefit reduces US tax by **>$500**

**Example:**
- Canada portion: $37,577
- US tax saved: $37,577 × 22% = $8,267
- **Form 8833 required** (>$500 threshold)

**Sample statement:**

> "I am claiming a treaty-based return position under Article XV(1) of the US-Canada Income Tax Treaty. Of the $100,000 RSU income reported on my W-2, $37,577 is attributable to employment services performed in Canada after I became a Canadian tax resident on July 1, 2025. This portion is exempt from US taxation. The remaining $62,423 attributable to services performed in the United States is reported as US-source income and is taxable in the US."

**Penalty for not filing:** $1,000

## Provincial Tax Considerations

### Choosing Your Canadian Province Strategically

Provincial tax rates vary significantly:

| Province | Top Marginal Rate | Tax on $100K RSU |
|----------|-------------------|------------------|
| Alberta | 48% (combined) | $38,000 |
| Ontario | 53.53% | $42,824 |
| BC | 53.5% | $42,800 |
| Quebec | 53.31% | $42,648 |
| Nova Scotia | 54% | $43,200 |

**Savings: Alberta vs Ontario**
- $42,824 - $38,000 = **$4,824/year**
- Over 4 years: **$19,296**

**But consider:**
- Cost of living (Alberta housing cheaper than Toronto/Vancouver)
- Job market (tech jobs concentrated in ON/BC)
- Quality of life (family, weather, culture)

**Tax optimization strategy:**
- Move to Alberta for 1-2 years (while RSUs vest)
- Establish residency (rent apartment, get AB driver's license)
- Save $20,000 in provincial tax
- Move to preferred province after RSUs fully vested

## Action Checklist

**When PR is approved:**
- [ ] Check COPR expiry date (1 year to land)
- [ ] Download all RSU vesting schedules (next 4 years)
- [ ] Calculate tax impact of landing now vs later (use our [calculator](/us-canada-tax-calculator))
- [ ] Ask employer about accelerated vesting options
- [ ] Ask employer about Canadian remote work (if preferred)

**Before landing in Canada:**
- [ ] Decide landing date (optimize for vesting schedule)
- [ ] File Form NR73 if doing "soft landing" (establish non-residency)
- [ ] Close unnecessary US ties (cancel gym, clubs if leaving permanently)
- [ ] Keep US ties if maintaining residency (apartment, car registration)

**After landing:**
- [ ] Track days in each country (for residency determination)
- [ ] Establish Canadian ties if becoming resident (home, bank, license)
- [ ] File dual-country returns for each year RSUs vest
- [ ] Claim Foreign Tax Credit (Form T2209 in Canada)
- [ ] File Form 8833 with US return (treaty benefits)

**Long-term (after RSUs fully vest):**
- [ ] Decide permanent tax residency (US vs Canada)
- [ ] File Form 8854 if renouncing US residency (exit tax implications)
- [ ] Close US brokerage accounts if no longer US tax resident
- [ ] Transfer investments to Canadian accounts (RRSP, TFSA)
